lead: A 3D computer graphics scene is built once and a camera path is chosen by an animator; the viewer watches a fixed film. VR closes a loop: trackers read the user's head and hands, the simulation updates, and the renderer draws a fresh view for each eye before the user notices the delay. That change from a spectator's picture to a participant's picture is the whole difference. It is used in surgical rehearsal, fire drills, machine training, building design review and rehabilitation.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the definition and 1.3 for why latency breaks immersion.

blocks.text: In 3D computer graphics, an artist builds geometry, materials and lights, then sets a camera path. The renderer may take seconds or minutes for one frame. The frames are stored and played back. The viewer is a spectator of an image the animator chose.

VR keeps the same geometry and rendering tools but changes who chooses the camera. Trackers report the user's pose: position (x, y, z) and orientation (yaw, pitch, roll). That is six degrees of freedom, or 6 DoF. The simulation updates the world, the renderer draws a left-eye and a right-eye view, the displays show them, and the user reacts. The loop from components is now closed.

The requirements follow from the loop: real-time rendering, stereo, a wide field of view, low latency, and 6 DoF tracking. Remove the loop and you have a 3D animation, not VR. See 1.1 for the boundary between VR and other XR forms.

At 90 Hz the display shows 90 frames each second. One frame budget is 1000 / 90 ≈ 11.1 ms. At 120 Hz it is 1000 / 120 ≈ 8.3 ms. All tracking, simulation and rendering for that frame must fit inside this budget. The budget is per frame, not per second.

blocks.where: refresh rate is the number of frames the display shows each second; the budget is the time allowed for one frame.

blocks.text: Motion-to-photon latency is the time from a real head movement to the light from the new view reaching the eye. It is the sum of tracking delay, simulation time, rendering time and display delay. A common target is under about 20 ms. Above that, the world swims behind the head and many users feel sick; see 1.3.

Stereo doubles the drawing work, and a wide field of view adds pixels. A dropped frame is visible as a stutter. Tracking types belong to Unit 2, displays to Unit 3, and the rendering pipeline to Unit 4.

sections.h3: What VR buys you, and what it costs

blocks.text: VR pays for its complexity in places where the real thing is costly, rare or unsafe.

items: Training with no risk and no consumables: a fire drill with no foam, a surgical step with no patient, a machine start-up with no scrap.
Seeing what is too big, too small, too far or too dangerous: a building before it is built, a molecule, a live power grid.
Remote presence: an expert inspects a site or guides a repair without travelling.
Rehabilitation and pain distraction: gentle reaching games, burn-care scenarios.
Education: a cell, a Diesel engine or a historical site at full scale.
Design review and prototyping: catch a clash before concrete is poured, which saves money.

blocks.text: The limits are real. A headset costs more than a monitor. Cybersickness appears when latency or optical mismatch is bad. Physical feedback is missing, so a virtual drill has no weight or kickback. Content takes skilled effort to build. Human factors and safety are in Unit 5; AR limits differ because the real world stays visible, as 1.6 explains.

figure.caption: One frame at 90 Hz has 11.1 ms; simulation takes 2 ms and rendering 7 ms, the tracker-to-display path adds 4 ms, so motion-to-photon latency is 13 ms, under the 20 ms target. At 120 Hz the budget shrinks to 8.3 ms, so the same 9 ms of simulation plus rendering no longer fits.

spec.title: Frame budget and latency: 90 Hz vs 120 Hz
spec.aria: A timeline chart with six bars in milliseconds: the 90 Hz frame budget of 11.1 ms, the 9 ms of simulation plus rendering, the 120 Hz budget of 8.3 ms that the 9 ms overruns, the 4 ms tracker-to-display path, the resulting 13 ms latency, and the 20 ms target it stays under.

examples.question: A headset refreshes at 90 Hz. One frame therefore has 1000/90 ≈ 11.1 ms. In a test, simulation takes 2 ms, rendering takes 7 ms and the tracker-to-display path adds 4 ms. (a) What is the motion-to-photon latency? (b) Does it meet a 20 ms target? (c) At 120 Hz the frame budget falls to 1000/120 ≈ 8.3 ms. The same 9 ms of simulation plus rendering no longer fits. Explain the result.
steps: Frame budget at 90 Hz = 1000 / 90 = 11.111 ms ≈ 11.1 ms.
Latency = simulation + rendering + tracker-to-display path = 2 + 7 + 4 = 13 ms.
Compare with the target: 13 ms < 20 ms, so it meets the target.
Frame budget at 120 Hz = 1000 / 120 = 8.333 ms ≈ 8.3 ms.
Simulation plus rendering = 2 + 7 = 9 ms. Since 9 ms > 8.3 ms, one frame cannot finish in one refresh period; frames are dropped and the view stutters.
examples.answer: The latency is 13 ms, which meets a 20 ms target; at 120 Hz the budget is 8.3 ms, so the same 9 ms of simulation plus rendering does not fit.

traps: Calling any 3D graphics seen in a headset VR. The marks are for the closed real-time loop, two eye views, and the latency budget; a pre-rendered walkthrough at 5 frames per second is 3D graphics.
Confusing refresh rate with latency. 90 Hz gives a frame budget of 1000/90 ≈ 11.1 ms, not 90 ms, and motion-to-photon latency is a separate sum.
Counting 6 DoF wrongly. It is three position values plus three orientation angles, not six position sensors or six separate trackers.
Treating low latency as optional. Examiners want the loop, stereo, 6 DoF tracking and a motion-to-photon target under roughly 20 ms.

quiz.q: Define six degrees of freedom for a VR headset.
quiz.a: Three position values (x, y, z) plus three orientation angles (yaw, pitch, roll); total 6.

quiz.q: Why must the camera pose in VR come from the user rather than an animator?
quiz.a: VR is a closed loop: the view must match the tracked head so the user's motion changes the image immediately; an animator's path makes the viewer a spectator.

quiz.q: A display refreshes at 72 Hz. Find the frame budget in milliseconds.
Simulation takes 3 ms, rendering takes 6 ms, and the tracker-to-display path takes 5 ms. Find the latency. Does it meet 20 ms? At 120 Hz, does 9 ms of simulation plus rendering fit?
quiz.a: Latency = 3 + 6 + 5 = 14 ms. Yes, 14 < 20 ms. At 120 Hz the budget is 1000/120 ≈ 8.3 ms, so 9 ms does not fit.

quiz.q: A pre-rendered 3D walkthrough runs at 5 frames per second and lets the user look around with key presses. Why is it not VR?
quiz.a: There is no continuous tracked pose, no per-eye real-time rendering tied to head motion, and the motion-to-photon delay is huge; it is 3D graphics played back.

quiz.q: Give three benefits and one limit of VR.
quiz.a: Benefits: safe training with no risk or consumables; seeing things too big, small or dangerous; design review that saves money. Limit: headset cost, cybersickness, missing physical feedback or content effort.

quiz.q: Why can a 120 Hz headset demand more optimisation than a 90 Hz one?
quiz.a: The frame budget drops from 11.1 ms to 8.3 ms; the same scene must finish sooner or frames drop, so a smoother display is harder to feed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern headsets use foveated rendering, where only the gaze region is drawn at full detail, to buy back frame time. Varifocal and light-field displays try to fix the vergence-accommodation conflict that causes eye strain. Research measures motion-to-photon latency with photodiodes and high-speed cameras, not by feel. Pass-through cameras blur the line between VR and video see-through AR. Search for 'foveated rendering', 'motion-to-photon measurement' and 'vergence-accommodation conflict'.
